papers.title: MusicListenBench: Can Audio LLMs Hear the Difference Yet?
papers.abstract: Audio large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on song genre, mood, and instrumentation. A more basic skill is telling whether two short clips play the same melody, chord or instrument. We introduce MusicListenBench, a benchmark of paired listening tests for melody, harmony, timbre, and tempo. Each test item comes with two variants. A FLIP variant changes the music, so the answer must change. A STAY variant changes only the sound, such as room echo or hiss, so the answer must stay the same. The two variants have opposite answers, so a model that ignores the audio scores 50%, whatever letter it prefers. The benchmark has a training split and two test sets, one rendered from symbolic music with exact labels and one built from real recordings. On the rendered test, seven of eight open audio LLMs score within 4 points of this floor. Of four commercial models, both GPT-Audio models are at chance, and the best, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 74.2%, 12.8 points below human listeners (87.0%). Post-training with GRPO on 10k rendered clean pairs raises Qwen2.5-Omni from 61.2% to 99.0% on held-out clean pairs, and the gain transfers to a task left out of training. On FLIP/STAY, however, it only reaches the level of our listeners (86.0%). It now misses almost no change (1.9%, against 24.7% for Gemini 2.5 Pro), yet when only the sound changes, it turns a correct answer into a wrong one 25.7\% of the time. More than half of its false flips come from a quiet background hiss. Models learn to hear a difference much faster than they learn which differences matter. On real recordings, open models again stay near chance, and the trained model calls 27 of 42 pairs of two strums of the same chord different. Adding sound-only pairs to training lowers false flips on both test sets, but no training run teaches relative pitch. We release the data, code, and an open leaderboard.

papers.title: Can Speech LLMs Recognize When Audio Evidence Is Insufficient? A Diagnostic Study and a Pre-Generation Probing Mitigation
papers.abstract: Speech large language models are usually evaluated on questions that have answers. We ask what they do when a recording establishes none, and whether the standard way of finding out is sound. Diagnosed on synthesized speech the answer looks clear: Qwen2-Audio fabricates an answer to 92.5% of unanswerable questions, while an ASR cascade reading the same recordings reaches 2.5% hallucination at 6.7% over-refusal, placing the failure in reasoning rather than in perception. The identical protocol on 376 native SQuAD 2.0 questions over human-read recordings removes that conclusion: the cascade hallucinates on 67.7% against the end-to-end model's 69.8%, at a higher over-refusal cost. A paired subset asking the same questions of a synthesized and a human recording of each passage localises the effect in the ASR stage -- the end-to-end model's abstention behaviour does not move with the speaker, the cascade's goes from 11.1% to 65.9%. Reliance on synthesized speech has been named as a limitation of audio benchmarks but not quantified; we quantify it, and show it large enough to reverse a finding. Since no prompt we tested repairs the residual failure, we transfer pre-generation attention probing to the multimodal setting. A probe over frozen prompt representations reaches 0.773 AUROC at predicting which unanswerable questions the model will answer anyway, where semantic entropy over ten sampled generations is at chance: the model fabricates the same answer every time, so sample disagreement cannot see a failure it is confident about.

papers.title: S$2$SCORE: A Textless Unified Evaluation Metric for Speech-to-Speech Translation Systems
papers.abstract: Evaluating speech-to-speech translation (S$2$ST) systems requires assessing multiple dimensions of translated speech, including semantic adequacy, speaker similarity, and acoustic naturalness. Existing approaches are largely text-based, relying on ASR transcripts and primarily assessing semantic adequacy, while other dimensions require separate metrics. We propose S$2$SCORE, a unified text-free evaluation framework that jointly models these dimensions within a multi-task architecture and produces a human-calibrated overall quality score. S$2$SCORE is trained using supervision derived from established evaluation models, enabling scalable learning without direct human annotations. Evaluated across five language pairs, S$2$SCORE shows strong agreement with human judgments, independent reference metrics, and the training supervision metrics, indicating robust generalization. The reference-free variant, S$2$SCORE-QE, consistently outperforms S$2$SCORE-REF and achieves stronger semantic adequacy prediction than BLASER~$2.0$.

papers.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincar\'e phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.

papers.title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models
papers.abstract: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that makes language modeling harder. Unified tokenizers combine both, but representing acoustic detail and linguistic content within a single feature space can cause interference between the two objectives, and existing approaches typically align acoustic representations to fixed semantic targets from a frozen teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified tokenization framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches aligned by a shared-index mechanism. This design learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code sequence, and it jointly optimizes both encoders without relying on fixed semantic teacher targets. Based on BiSAT, we develop BiSAT-TTS, a zero-shot text-to-speech system comprising an autoregressive text-speech LM and a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder. Reconstruction, downstream understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT effectively preserves semantic and acoustic information in the code stream, performs well on in-the-wild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary codebook representations. The frozen-code understanding results also support its feasibility and potential for code-based reward modeling in reinforcement learning post-training. BiSAT-TTS performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech LM-based TTS baselines with less training data, further supporting BiSAT's effectiveness for speech language modeling. The audio demos are available at https://seekmind-lab.github.io/bisat-demo.

papers.title: PAWP-TTS: Phoneme-Aware Weight Programming for Compact Bilingual English-Nepali Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: This paper presents PAWP-TTS, a compact non-autoregressive text-to-speech system for English, Nepali, and English-Nepali code-mixed speech at 24 kHz, with no language model at inference. Deterministic pronunciation knowledge lives in a rule- and lexicon-based bilingual frontend that preserves native Nepali contrasts and avoids Hindi phonology, so the network only models acoustics. Counting every learned inference tensor, including the waveform decoder, PAWP-1.5M (1,490,390 parameters, 5.98 MB) reaches 1.50% English and 1.75% Nepali character error rate under a single ASR recognizer, and 5.04% / 4.02% Nepali / English phoneme error rate (PER) on 600 untouched test utterances. Decoder-centric 281K-parameter models (1.1 MB) stay intelligible across three independent seeds, with equal-budget dense models (5.53 +/- 0.08% NE, 5.34 +/- 0.28% EN PER) outperforming K=2 cross-layer shared-basis models (6.35 +/- 0.11% NE, 6.57 +/- 0.47% EN PER). Fixing a frontend/label version mismatch nearly halved Nepali PER, more than any architectural or weight-level change. The paper then studies weight-space programming: inspection-guided, zero-training weight edits. Under strict controls (validation-only selection, one-shot test, paired bootstrap, matched random and same-parameter gradient baselines), edits show real selectivity (27:1 on word-boundary pauses with 96 weights; zero cross-lingual collateral inside language-gated residuals) but no accuracy gain beyond controls. Two apparent targets proved to be label or phonology artifacts. Code, ONNX graphs, and CC BY 4.0 weights are released.

papers.title: Restorable Multilingual Voice Anonymization via Audio Watermarking
papers.abstract: Voice anonymization aims to conceal speaker identity while preserving linguistic and paralinguistic information. However, certain applications also require the ability to attribute anonymized recordings to their original speakers. Existing recovery approaches often rely on specially designed reversible anonymization systems, limiting their applicability to different anonymization architectures. In this work, we propose a post-hoc framework for restorable multilingual voice anonymization that enables speaker attribution without reconstructing the original waveform or modifying the underlying anonymization systems. Specifically, we convert 192-dimensional speaker embeddings into binary identity payloads through sign quantization and embed them into anonymized speech using a segment-wise audio watermarking strategy. Recovered payloads are subsequently matched against enrollment speaker templates for identity attribution. We evaluate the framework across four languages using two distinct anonymization backbones, BM1 and T24. Under clean conditions, the approach achieves approximately 99% exact payload recovery and 0.96% attribution EER while largely preserving the original privacy-utility performance. Experiments further show that speaker attribution remains reliable under several audio distortions despite imperfect payload recovery, although temporal rescaling severely disrupts recovery. Additional analyses reveal that watermark robustness varies across languages, carrier durations, and anonymization backbones.

papers.title: From Spatial Perception to Speech Recovery: Binaural Semantic Adaptation for Spatially Grounded Multi-Talker Transcription
papers.abstract: Spatial audio large language models increasingly combine general audio understanding with spatial perception. Yet overlapping conversations require more than locating speakers. A model must also recover what each person says and match the words to their positions. We examine this challenge in MiDashengLM-Spatial, a binaural model designed for both spatial reasoning and general audio understanding. To test these abilities, we introduce BiCP-Bench, a benchmark of overlapping two-speaker binaural recordings that contrasts candidate-based recognition, position-guided transcription, and joint transcription with spatial attribution. The model can identify a target utterance among candidates but struggles to transcribe it without them. Its semantic encoder uses only one ear. Changing that ear shifts which side's speech is recovered more accurately, despite unchanged binaural input to the spatial branch. We therefore propose Binaural Semantic Adaptation (BiSA), which combines shared encoding of both ears with cross-ear differential interactions. With the backbone frozen and 0.027% trainable parameters, BiSA raises correctly attributed joint transcription success from 0% to 57.81% for simultaneous onsets. For staggered onsets, later-speaker word error rate falls from 109.47% to 29.58%. On full-length Clarity CEC1 mixtures, word error rate falls from 59.33% to 39.60%. Spatial reasoning on MMAU-Pro improves by 9.54 percentage points without updating the spatial encoder, and general audio performance remains largely intact.

papers.title: Beyond File-Level Splits: Rethinking Symbolic Music Evaluation via Multi-View Alignment
papers.abstract: Symbolic music generation often continues MIDI passages by predicting subsequent notes or events. Held-out prediction loss can overestimate generalization to unseen compositions when training contains another performance or arrangement of a test work. We introduce Multi-View Alignment-Aware Same-Work Identification, combining complementary musical representations with temporal alignment of shared passages to remove test-work versions from training while preserving unrelated material and fixing evaluation files. In a controlled cohort of 100 manually verified pairs selected for high embedding similarity, replacing 3.29% of training windows with test-work versions reduces mean per-group NLL by up to 30.16% relative to matched unrelated content. Across two datasets and two generators, our method brings test losses closest to a reference built from independent work labels. Compared with removing the same number of files at random, it leaves fewer test works exposed and retains more eligible content, including about 99% of eligible tokens on the piano-performance dataset. A separate study on that dataset matches training tokens and updates: no test works remain exposed under the dataset labels, and mean relative test loss is 2.15% higher than an independently selected reference. These findings support keeping all versions of each composition in one split when evaluating generalization to unseen works. The project is available at https://kunbai05-nb.github.io/.

papers.title: EdgeALM: An Efficient and Unified Edge Accelerator for Large Audio Language Models via Full-Stack Hardware-Software Co-Design and Agent-Driven Recursive Optimization
papers.abstract: Edge deployment of audio language models (ALMs) is constrained by large model footprints, heterogeneous workloads, and limited software support. This paper presents EdgeALM, an efficient and unified FPGA accelerator for ALMs that combines full-stack hardware-software co-design with agent-driven recursive optimization. An end-to-end ALM compression flow is developed, combining a unified AWQ-style quantizer with modality-conditioned vocabulary pruning. A Conv-Matmul Disaggregation architecture is proposed, with dedicated matrix and convolution engines that operate concurrently on their respective workloads. An Extra-Coarse-Grained ISA is designed to incorporate regular on-chip data movement and execution sequences into compute instructions, reducing software complexity with modest hardware control overhead. Hardware and software recursive loops are introduced for agent-driven full-stack optimization. The proposed EdgeALM is implemented on a single Alveo U50 in an ordinary desktop PC and demonstrates inference on more than 20 models, including ALMs with up to 13B parameters within the 8-GB HBM capacity. It achieves high-throughput audio-to-text inference at up to 169.5 tokens/s and sustains real-time streaming audio-to-audio inference, with 94% bandwidth utilization and 26 W power consumption on average. Standalone ASR, text-only LLM, and TTS models are also well supported, and can be combined in cascades. Compared with state-of-the-art FPGA accelerators (e.g., EdgeLLM), EdgeALM scales to larger models and supports a wider range of inference workloads extended to the audio modality, while achieving higher bandwidth utilization at lower board power and cost.

papers.title: Characterizing Frozen SSL Encoders and Backends for Cross-Domain Speech Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) encoders are the dominant front end for speech deepfake detection, and the prevailing recipe fine-tunes the full encoder on a small spoofing corpus, maximizing in-domain accuracy at the cost of known degradation under domain shift. Taking a recent cross-attention fusion of SSL and constant-Q cepstral features as a fixed reference recipe, we freeze its encoder and ask which encoder and which backend behave best across domains. We cross two frozen encoders, the massively multilingual XEUS and Wav2Vec2 XLSR-53, with two backends, multi-head factorized attentive (MHFA) pooling and AASIST, and evaluate on ASVspoof 2019 LA, ASVspoof 2021 LA and DF, In-the-Wild (ITW), and ASVspoof 5, training every system in one pipeline over three seeds. We report three findings. First, encoder and backend interact: MHFA suits the stronger encoder, while AASIST recovers more from and stabilizes the weaker one. Second, within this recipe, the frozen encoder produces large, repeatable differences. With MHFA, frozen XEUS lowers error relative to frozen XLSR-53 by 58-77% on LA21, DF21, and ASV5, and more modestly on ITW. This ordering persists in a matched-aggregation ablation, and a capacity-matched WavLM Large diagnostic shows that parameter count alone does not explain XLSR-53's weaker performance. Third, against a three-seed fine-tuned baseline, frozen XEUS updates under 0.4M parameters versus 316M, wins on ASVspoof 5 (in EER and min-DCF) and modestly on LA21, trails on DF21 and ITW, and shows lower seed variation on three of the four out-of-domain sets.

papers.title: Training speech deepfake detectors against worst-case filters: Gains, Costs and Limits
papers.abstract: Speech deepfake detectors make few errors on standard benchmarks, yet a simple attack defeats them: the attacker passes fake speech through one short filter, tuned against the detector, and many fakes then pass as real. Training with random filters does not stop this attack, because the attacker uses the worst filter, not a random one. We therefore train the detector against the worst case: during training, a small set of filters is updated to fool the current detector, at about the cost of random filters. In a preregistered study, this made the detector more robust to filter attacks on real-world recordings than random filters did. It also lowered the in-domain attack error of the standard detector, and beat one-step adversarial training with additive noise on real-world recordings. The price is a higher error on unfiltered speech, and a validation study shows that choosing the checkpoint on held-out spoofing systems made the standard detector about as robust.

papers.title: When Being Wrong Is Right: Reverse-Capability Audio CAPTCHAs through Psychoacoustic Design
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have recently been shown to bypass audio CAPTCHAs designed around limitations of automatic speech recognition. To address this threat, we introduce reverse-capability verification, a general CAPTCHA framework that reverses the conventional human-easy, machine-hard relationship with respect to the physical ground truth. It selects challenges in which stable human perceptual limitations cause the human-reference answer to differ from the physical ground truth, while machine analysis tends toward that truth. Because the verifier accepts the human-reference answer, advanced solver capabilities and resulting improved recovery of the physical ground truth may instead strengthen the human-machine separation. We instantiate the framework through psychoacoustics and design two audio CAPTCHAs: HIPI, a classification task, and YINGCHEN, a counting task, together with their conjunctive composition. Across seven LALMs and eight attack strategies, the maximum observed machine acceptance rates are 19%, 17%, and 3% for HIPI, YINGCHEN, and their composition, respectively, compared with 45-100% for nine prior schemes. A multidimensional human usability study yields corresponding human acceptance rates of 78%, 90%, and 76%, while maintaining competitive efficiency and satisfaction. Further analysis demonstrates that advanced LALMs tend toward physical ground truth. These results show that reverse-capability verification substantially reduces machine acceptance while retaining high human acceptance through an approach different from conventional CAPTCHAs.

papers.title: Ultrasound Watermark: Real-time Acoustic Watermarking against Voice Scams on Smartphones
papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and AI-driven speech synthesis enable adversaries to convincingly impersonate trusted individuals during phone calls. Existing defenses often rely on offline analysis, degrade under telephony distortions, or remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. To address these limitations, we present Ultrasound Watermark, a real-time, smartphone-native framework that protects live calls by binding speech to the caller's physical articulatory motion through acoustic watermarking. During a call, the smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures reflections from facial articulatory movements using only its built-in speaker and microphone. Ultrasound Watermark extracts motion features from these reflections and fuses them with outgoing speech to generate a dynamic watermark. Because the ultrasonic measurements are physically and temporally coupled with speech production, they are difficult to spoof without the underlying articulatory motion. A synchronized generator-detector architecture enforces cross-modal speech-motion consistency against replay, synthesized speech, and articulation-mimicking attacks. Ultrasound Watermark operates continuously with less than 200 ms latency overhead and requires no additional hardware. We implement Ultrasound Watermark on iOS and Android and evaluate it using over 2.5 hours of synchronized speech-ultrasound recordings from 22 speakers across eight smartphones and four real-world environments. Results demonstrate robustness to diverse attacks and telephony distortions while preserving perceptual audio quality.

papers.title: LiveAudio: From Bidirectional to Autoregressive Diffusion for Real-Time Streaming Video-to-Audio Generation
papers.abstract: Video-to-audio generation synthesizes sound that matches a video in content and timing, with applications ranging from film post-production to live streaming, games and interactive world models. Interactive applications receive video continuously and need the sound to follow it in real time, yet most existing video-to-audio models are bidirectional and must observe an entire clip before producing any sound. We propose LiveAudio, a streaming video-to-audio framework that generates high-quality and synchronized audio in real time while the video is playing. In contrast to prior streaming models trained from scratch, LiveAudio converts a bidirectional model into a streaming generator so as to build on its audio quality and synchronization. LiveAudio generates audio block by block, and each block depends only on the video that has already been played. The streaming generator is obtained from the bidirectional model through progressive causal fine-tuning and distillation, so that each block needs only a few sampling steps. Experiments on VGGSound show that LiveAudio outperforms existing streaming models in audio quality and synchronization, and surpasses the bidirectional model it starts from in synchronization. On a single A100 GPU, it runs in real time with a real-time factor of 0.79 and a time to first frame of 143 ms. Audio samples are available at https://streamaudio.github.io.

papers.title: Music Circuit: Trace and Control Style Dynamics in Large Music Generation Model
papers.abstract: Musical style, a global attribute that functions throughout a whole piece, is a lever widely used by users in modern large music generation models. Yet how style is represented inside these models, and which components drive it, remains largely unexplored. In language models, circuit analysis traces a representation to a sparse sub-network of a few key components, namely attention heads and MLP neurons, and has been used successfully to explain and control global attributes such as emotion. In this work, we use circuit analysis to study the mechanisms behind musical style. Based on YuE2, we build a dataset that pairs the same lyrics with five styles and design a three-step framework. First, stage localization shows that the style forms mainly in the score-planning stage. Second, static observation across the positions of this stage further reveals that style is not a fixed vector but a dynamic representation across tokens. Third, we therefore merge the activation differences across positions into one direction per style, and trace the neurons and attention heads that drive this direction into a sparse circuit. Without any style text, steering this circuit successfully transfers one piece into the target style, matching and even exceeding the style prompt. To our knowledge, this is the first work to analyze and control musical style at the circuit level in a large music generation model. Audio and score examples are available at https://aristo233.github.io/Music_Circuit/.

papers.title: Synthetic Twins: Closing the Gap Between TTS Test Sets and Real Recordings in Turkish ASR Evaluation
papers.abstract: Speech synthesized by text-to-speech engines is a low-cost substitute for recorded test sets in automatic speech recognition, yet an off-the-shelf synthetic test set is worth only a few dozen real recordings for estimating the real error rate of a recognizer. This paper examines which properties of real recordings are missing from synthetic speech and how much of the gap can be closed. For 507 Turkish Common Voice recordings, synthetic twins are built: a ladder of synthetic copies that adds, one factor at a time, the pitch of the speaker, a clone of the same speaker, the real recording channel and the speaking rate. At each step, the agreement between ASR behaviour on the copy and on the real recording is measured. Across three zero-shot cloning engines and panels of six and 19 recognizers, the speaker clone is the step that improves agreement on which sentences are hard, raising the Spearman correlation from .41 to .55 for Chatterbox. Matching the channel or adding generic noise corrects the error level when the synthetic speech is easier than real speech. The twin with the highest worth is equivalent to 70 to 122 real recordings, depending on the recognizer panel, compared with about 9 for a stock voice. The findings replicate on VoxForge, a second corpus in which speaker identity is known rather than inferred: the clone raises sentence agreement from .31 to .50 and the worth from 8 to about 50 recordings. Agreement on which sentences are hard is distinct from agreement on how hard they are. The paper concludes with a practical recipe and a reporting checklist for synthetic ASR test sets.

papers.title: IteraSong: LLM-Guided Iterative Symbolic Music Creation in a Web DAW
papers.abstract: Music creation is inherently iterative, yet many symbolic generation systems still center on producing or regenerating isolated outputs. We present IteraSong, an interactive web-based Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) for LLM-guided iterative symbolic music creation. Unlike one-shot generation systems, IteraSong supports a generate-audition-edit-refine loop over a persistent multi-track project. Users initialize a fully labeled pop draft, then progressively refine it through natural-language instructions. The LLM maps requests to a hierarchical action space of editing primitives exposed via Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, spanning global, track, section, and bar/note scopes. The demo enables attendees to edit multi-track compositions in natural language, apply deterministic and generative edits, and undo/redo changes in real time.

papers.title: Which Layer to Trust? Layer Selection in Frozen Speech Encoders for Singing-Voice Deepfake Detection under Signal Corruption
papers.abstract: Frozen self-supervised speech encoders have been frequently used for audio deepfake detection. However, the layers are usually chosen from a development set. We examine this choice for singing-voice deepfake detection on CtrSVDD. We train one detection head per layer, plus a learned layer mix, on frozen XEUS (3-4 seeds) and XLS-R (2 seeds). We test on clean audio and under noise, reverberation and lossy coding. On clean audio, the middle layers beat the last layer in both encoders and the learned mix does not beat the best single layer. The layer chosen on the development set is 2.3 (XEUS) and 4.1 (XLS-R) percentage points of EER worse than the best test layer. Under noise and coding, XEUS's best layers stay in the middle, while under reverberation its upper layers catch up, whereas XLS-R's best layer moves shallower. In an exploratory analysis, XEUS detects a commercial synthesis attack best with an earlier layer, especially under noise. The layer therefore cannot be chosen reliably on an in-domain development set and clean audio alone.

papers.title: SpeechSplice: Pronunciation Control in Encoder-Decoder LLM-based TTS by Replacing Encoder Hidden States
papers.abstract: Most large language model (LLM)-based text-to-speech (TTS) methods offer no explicit function for correcting pronunciation. Consequently, these systems frequently mispronounce many everyday words, such as proper nouns, heteronyms, numerals, and domain-specific terms. While weight-editing or fine-tuning can mitigate this, these solutions risk quality degradation and must operate offline. We propose SpeechSplice, a training-free encoder-output replacement approach for pronunciation control in encoder-decoder LLM-based TTS. SpeechSplice replaces the encoder-output hidden states of a word with those of its intended reading. Cross-architecture and cross-lingual experiments cover ten public TTS systems in 17 model-language conditions. At the hidden state we replace, the intervention moves pronunciation toward the target reading more often when the generator reads the text through cross-attention than when text and speech share one self-attention sequence. In human evaluations, native-language listeners identified speech generated with SpeechSplice as realizing the target reading in 98.6-100.0% of judgments, while a separate study found no significant naturalness difference from unmodified synthesis. By clarifying the conditions under which pronunciation correction succeeds, this study offers an empirical basis for investigating pronunciation control in LLM-based TTS architectures.

papers.title: Scoring L2 Pronunciation Without Synthesis: Counterfactual Velocity Contrast in Frozen Flow-Matching TTS
papers.abstract: Flow-matching text-to-speech (TTS) models learn how native speakers realize a text, yet this knowledge is used only for synthesis. We show that a frozen TTS model can score non-native (L2) pronunciation without generating audio. For a learner utterance, we compare the model's velocity-prediction error under the target text with its error under a counterfactual text (dropped or swapped) on the same noised input; the difference behaves like a generative goodness-of-pronunciation score. The signal is confined to a narrow band of high-noise timesteps, which a native-speech criterion locates and a closed-form rule transfers across backbones. On speaker-disjoint speechocean762, four frozen TTS models reach $r{=}0.58$--$0.63$ with human scores, within the range of zero-shot ASR and phone-level baselines, and adding them to those baselines in a label-free fusion raises $r$ from $0.698$ to $0.757$. Cached frame scores also flag word-level errors at no extra TTS cost.

papers.title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech
papers.abstract: Speaking early turns a prediction into an irreversible public commitment. We introduce SayWhen, a test-time controller that selects a task-directed act shared across typed continuation plans and controls its release as speech. A persistent veto blocks playback when intervening transcripts invalidate the candidate. We define regret-free early speech (RFES) to measure supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility. On a 72-prefix branching diagnostic, the generated-plan frontier attains 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret, versus 8.2% RFES and 0.068 regret for Matched Top-One. Measured planner latency constrains this path; a deterministic retail schema attains 31.7% RFES, compared with 32.0% for the complete policy. In a separate 30-task $\tau$-Voice simulation, schema-derived candidates with cached text-to-speech (TTS) audio attain 21/30 task-level RFES. Eligible audio begins 1.51 seconds before the user-audio endpoint among the 22 tasks with early speech, or 1.11 seconds over all 30 tasks with zero for tasks without eligible early speech. Semantic veto and endpoint waiting each pass 16/30 tasks. Together, the studies demonstrate a controlled coverage-compatibility trade-off and schema-based pre-endpoint operation, making the supported public commitment an explicit unit of voice-agent control.

papers.title: Tenlai-TTS 2.0: Continuous-Representation LLM-Based TTS System with End-to-End Training
papers.abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) with continuous speech latents avoids quantization-induced information loss, but typically relies on a latent space that is learned separately and then frozen before language-model training. Such a space must satisfy two competing requirements: it must retain enough acoustic detail for high-fidelity reconstruction, yet be sufficiently structured and regularized to support autoregressive prediction by a language model. We present Tenlai-TTS 2.0, which learns continuous speech representations through end-to-end training to balance acoustic detail with autoregressive predictability. The model comprises a speech encoder with a capacity-controlled Gaussian bottleneck, a large language model (LLM) with an autoregressive diffusion transformer (AR-DiT) head, a flow-matching (FM) mel-spectrogram decoder, and a multi-task recognition model (RM). With energy normalization and fixed-variance Gaussian noise, the bottleneck has a closed-form upper bound on its information rate. Through joint optimization with reconstruction, recognition, and next-patch prediction objectives, we learn continuous speech representations that suit all three tasks and train the LLM and AR-DiT for autoregressive generation. The LLM and AR-DiT are further optimized using differentiable reconstruction and recognition feedback on their predicted latents through the FM decoder and RM. On Seed-TTS-eval, this feedback-based optimization reduces character error rate (CER) from 0.82% to 0.74% on test-zh and from 8.32% to 7.08% on test-hard-zh, and word error rate (WER) from 1.32% to 1.27% on test-en, compared with joint training alone. Subsequent reinforcement learning further reduces CER to 6.29% on test-hard-zh and WER to 1.08% on test-en, with speaker similarity scores of 0.811, 0.766, and 0.784 on test-zh, test-en, and test-hard-zh, respectively.

Sori-10B-Speech

Seonuk Kim  ·  Semin Kim  ·  Beom Jun Woo  ·  🇰🇷
{sukim, smkim21, bjwoo}@hi.snu.ac.kr

*Sori* (소리) is Korean for *sound*. Sori-10B-Speech is a speech LLM that hears how things are said (tone, hesitation, emotion, who is speaking and in what state) and uses those cues when it reasons. ## Usage ```python # pip install "transformers>=5.23" soundfile import soundfile as sf import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor repo = "snkii/Sori-10B-Speech" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(repo, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto") audio, sr = sf.read("speech.wav", dtype="float32") # 16 kHz mono messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": "How does the speaker sound, and why?"}, ]}] prompt = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False) inputs = processor(text=prompt, audio=audio, sampling_rate=sr, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256) print(processor.decode(output[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)) ``` Reasoning before answering: the model first writes down what it hears, then answers. ```python prompt = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False, enable_thinking=True) inputs = processor(text=prompt, audio=audio, sampling_rate=sr, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, do_sample=True, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20) text = processor.decode(output[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True) reasoning, _, answer = text.partition("") print(answer.strip()) ``` Several clips and questions in one batch: ```python files = ["a.wav", "b.wav", "c.wav"] questions = ["How does the speaker sound, and why?", "What is the speaker's mood?", "Is the speaker hesitant?"] audios = [sf.read(f, dtype="float32")[0] for f in files] # 16 kHz mono prompts = [processor.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": q}, ]}], add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False) for q in questions] inputs = processor(text=prompts, audio=audios, sampling_rate=16000, padding=True, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256) for answer in processor.batch_decode(output[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True): print(answer) ``` ## License Sori-10B-Speech is released under **[CC BY-NC-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/)**: use it and build on it for non-commercial purposes, with attribution, and share what you derive from it under the same terms. Commercial use is not licensed because part of the training data is licensed for non-commercial use. Third-party components keep their own licenses, which will be listed with the weights. ## Citation ```bibtex @software{kim_sori_10b_speech_2026, author = {Kim, Seonuk and Kim, Semin and Woo, Beom Jun}, title = {{Sori-10B-Speech}}, year = {2026}, institution = {Human Interface Laboratory, Seoul National University}, url = {https://huggingface.co/snkii/Sori-10B-Speech} } ```

Talk to it, interrupt it, turn on your camera. > **No GPU?** Try it through the hosted API: [sign up](https://api.adventists.ai/console/) and get 3 hours of free voice chat (OpenAI Realtime-compatible, [docs](https://api.adventists.ai/console/docs)). **Version 1.4.0** (2026-11-16) · [changelog](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) · [GitHub](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime) > **On a Mac?** [Sophon-Realtime-4B-Flash-MLX](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-4B-Flash-MLX) runs this build locally on Apple silicon Macs with 16 GB or more (MLX; new in 1.5.0). The 4B member of the Sophon-Realtime family: the same full-duplex design as the 32B builds, on **one 24 GB GPU (uses ~21 GB)**. It listens while you talk, decides from your voice when you have finished, writes a reply with sound tags (`[laughter]` `[cough]` `[sigh]` `[breath]` `…`) and speaks while it writes; a lighter, faster speech model speaks the tagged reply (one forward pass per 80 ms frame). Served as **one** vLLM-Omni model, with `/v1/realtime` and `/v1/chat/completions`. ## Sophon-Realtime 4B: three builds, one 4B brain | | **Tag** | **Flash** | **E2E** | |---|---|---|---| | How it speaks | an expressive speech model (tag-tts) performs the sound tags | a lighter, faster speech model speaks the tagged reply (one forward pass per 80 ms frame) | a compact talker (about 350M parameters) turns the tagged reply straight into voice vectors; a decoder turns them into sound | | Runs on | one 32 GB GPU (uses ~27 GB) | one 24 GB GPU (uses ~21 GB) | one 32 GB GPU (uses ~31 GB) | | Full-Duplex-Bench v1.0 (4-task avg) | 94.3 | 87.7 | 92.3 | | First audio, one user (RTX PRO 6000) | 0.4 s | 0.21 s | 0.31 s | | Weights | [HF](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-4B-Tag) · [ModelScope](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-4B-Tag) | [HF](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-4B-Flash) · [ModelScope](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-4B-Flash) | [HF](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-4B-E2E) · [ModelScope](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-4B-E2E) | The 4B brain is [DuplexJev-4B-Para](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para), our open 4B speech model, with a tag-writing adapter merged in. Speech only: the 4B brain has no vision. For the strongest answers, use the 32B builds ([Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag) · [Flash](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash) · [E2E](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E)) or the [hosted API](https://api.adventists.ai/console/). ## Benchmarks | | 4B | 32B (published) | |---|---|---| | VoiceBench overall | 62.4 | 82.8 | | Big Bench Audio (spoken answer, transcribed) | 44.3% | 81.8% | | Full-Duplex-Bench v1.0, Flash build (avg of 2 pause tasks, turn-taking, interruption) | 87.7 | 94.0 | | Sound-tag rate on held-out conversations (reference: 0.36) | 0.36 | — | **What 4B is for.** The 4B brain keeps the conversation skills of the family: listening while you talk, deciding when you have finished, back-channels, barge-in and sound tags (Full-Duplex-Bench close to the 32B builds, and the same tag rate as the reference data). It knows and reasons much less than the 32B brain (VoiceBench 62.4 vs 82.8, Big Bench Audio 44.3% vs 81.8%), so it can state wrong facts with confidence. Use it for local demos, companions and characters, and research on turn-taking; use the 32B builds or the hosted API when answers must be right. Among open full-duplex models, its VoiceBench score is above Freeze-Omni (55.2) and Moshi (29.5) and below MiniCPM-o (71.2). Measured 2026-11-16 on one RTX PRO 6000 with each build held to the memory of the card it is configured for. VoiceBench: official evaluators, gpt-4o-mini judge, AlpacaEval on the standard 199-question subset, overall = mean of 9 tasks. Big Bench Audio: 1,000 questions, GPT-4.1 judges the transcript of the spoken answer. Full-Duplex-Bench v1.0: average of candor and synthetic pause handling, turn-taking and user interruption (backchannel is reported but not averaged), the same scripts as for the 32B release. First audio: one user, `client_example.py`, median of 6. The 32B column repeats the numbers published for the 32B builds. ## Quick start ```bash git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime && cd sophon-realtime/flash bash install.sh # once: Python 3.12 venv, vLLM 0.30, vLLM-Omni 0.30, plugin modelscope download --model AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-4B-Flash --local_dir ./model # or: hf download adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-4B-Flash --local-dir ./model GPU=0 PORT=8000 bash start.sh # sees the 4B model and picks its 24 GB config python client_example.py --url http://127.0.0.1:8000 ``` Full instructions, the realtime protocol, zero-shot voice cloning and Live mode: [flash/README.md](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/flash/README.md). ## Layout `config.json` · `thinker/` (4B, bf16), `talker/`, `voices/` License: Apache-2.0; see `NOTICE` for the sources of the bundled weights. **Only clone your own voice or a voice you have permission to use.**

Talk to it, interrupt it, turn on your camera. > **No GPU?** Try it through the hosted API: [sign up](https://api.adventists.ai/console/) and get 3 hours of free voice chat (OpenAI Realtime-compatible, [docs](https://api.adventists.ai/console/docs)). > 🆕 **Smaller GPU?** [Sophon-Realtime-4B-Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-4B-Tag) (v1.4.0) runs this build with a 4B brain on one 32 GB GPU: keeps the turn-taking and sound tags, knows much less. [All builds](https://huggingface.co/collections/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime-6afb357253a3a8905ad758b0) **Version 1.2.0** (2026-11-13) · [changelog](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) · [▶ v1.1 demo video](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime#zero-shot-voice-cloning-new-in-v11) Code and one-command deployment: [github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/tree/main/tag](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/tree/main/tag) · Built on [DuplexJev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Voice: [tag-tts](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/tag-tts) **The Tag build of Sophon-Realtime: it decides how to say it, and runs on one GPU.** The 32B thinker listens to you, decides when it is its turn, and writes the reply together with inline sound tags: a laugh after a joke, a sigh for bad news, stress on the word that matters. A streaming voice (tag-tts) performs those tags while the reply is still being written. Tags are never read aloud and are removed from the text stream. The whole system is **one vLLM-Omni model**: thinker → tag-tts talker → flow + HiFT vocoder, on a single 80 GB GPU. ## Sophon-Realtime v1 family Three builds share one brain (the same 32B model listens, decides turns and writes the reply). They differ only in how the reply becomes sound. Full comparison: [github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime). | | **Tag** (recommended) | **Flash** | **E2E** | |---|---|---|---| | How it speaks | an expressive speech model performs the sound tags | a lighter, faster speech model speaks the tagged reply | a compact talker (about 350M parameters) generates continuous voice vectors directly, no speech tokens | | NVV-SuperBench (en / zh) | **0.80 / 0.86** | 0.63 / 0.77 | 0.75 / 0.85 | | First audio, one user | ~0.6 s | 0.31 s | **~0.25 s** | | Users per 80 GB GPU (recommended) | 16 | **40** | 16 | | GPUs | 1 | 1 | 1 | | Weights | [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag) | [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash) | [Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E) | Pick **Tag** if you want the voice to act; pick **Flash** if users per GPU matter most; pick **E2E** for the fastest first audio with a voice that still laughs and sighs. Tag and Flash share the same APIs; E2E runs on its own engine or, since 1.1.4, on vLLM-Omni with the same APIs as Tag and Flash. ## Highlights - **VoiceBench 82.8 and Big Bench Audio 81.8%: the strongest brain among open full-duplex models.** #1 among open full-duplex models on both; level with GPT-4o-mini-Audio on VoiceBench. - **Paralinguistic understanding 48.6, #1 overall: it hears your tone.** Ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (46.9) and Qwen3-Omni (44.6) on LISTEN, StressTest and MSPB. It hears emotion, emphasis, sarcasm, laughter and sighs straight from your voice. - **The most expressive build: NVV-SuperBench 0.86 (Chinese) and 0.80 (English).** The model decides when to laugh, sigh, breathe, clear its throat or stress a word; the voice performs it instead of reading the tag aloud. - **One 80 GB GPU, one command.** Served by vLLM-Omni; up to 16 concurrent users per GPU, about 0.6 s to first audio. - **Full-Duplex-Bench v3 tool calling: Pass@1 48%, ahead of Grok (43%), with a 100% response rate.** Live mode is compatible with the OpenAI GPT-Live interface. - **Real full duplex.** It listens the whole time you talk and drafts its reply as you go; it picks up when you stop, stops when you cut in, and keeps going when you just say "mm-hm". - **Apache-2.0, free for commercial use.** Fine-tune persona, tone and domain knowledge with ms-swift. Benchmark methods and full comparison tables: [v1 family home page](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-v1). To just try it: [talk to it in the ModelScope Studio](https://www.modelscope.ai/studios/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime). ## Deploy (one GPU, one command) ```bash git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime && cd sophon-realtime/tag bash install.sh # Python 3.12 venv, vLLM 0.30, vLLM-Omni 0.30, the plugin, and these weights (~42 GB) GPU=0 PORT=8000 bash start.sh # first start 15–20 min (kernels + TensorRT engines), later 5–8 min python client_example.py --wav my_question.wav --lang en --voice ryan_en ``` - APIs: `ws://HOST:8000/v1/realtime` (full duplex: turn-taking, barge-in, backchannel) and `POST /v1/chat/completions` (audio in → text + audio stream). - Voices: `chelsie` (default; `chelsie_zh` / `chelsie_en` picked by language), `vivian_zh`, `ryan_en`, `brand_zh`, `brand_en`. ## Zero-shot voice cloning (new in 1.1) Give it a short clip of any voice and talk to Sophon in that voice. No fine-tuning, no restart. ```bash cp alice.wav model/voices/alice.wav # 3–10 s of clean speech from one speaker (wav or flac, any sample rate) python client_example.py --wav my_question.wav --lang en --voice alice ``` - Use `"voice": "alice"` in `/v1/chat/completions` or in `session.update` on `/v1/realtime`. The clip can be in another language than the reply. - The server prepares new clips in the background within a few seconds, so first audio is as fast as with a built-in voice. Overwrite a file to replace a voice, delete it to remove it. Sound tags (laughs, sighs, …) work with cloned voices too. - 1.1 also updates the voice model (`talker/flow.pt` and its ONNX) so that unseen voices come out much closer to the reference. Needs the latest code: GitHub `main` or `pip install -U "sophon-realtime[trt]"` (1.1.0 or later). - **Only clone your own voice or a voice you have permission to use. Do not use it to impersonate or deceive anyone.** - Hardware: one 80 GB GPU (H100 / H800 / A100 80G), about 65 GB per instance. ## Performance (one H100 80 GB, measured) | Concurrent users (arriving within 10 s) | First audio, median / max | Stutter (median) | |---|---|---| | 1 | 0.67 s | ~0 | | 8 | 0.61 / 0.76 s | 0 | | **16** | **0.75 / 1.07 s** | 0.06 s | | 24 | 1.36 / 2.11 s | 0.39 s (queueing starts) | - Full duplex: about 0.7 s from the end of the user's speech to the first voice. - **These numbers need TensorRT.** `install.sh` installs it; with pip, install `pip install "sophon-realtime[trt]"` (CUDA 13). Without TensorRT the voice runs in plain PyTorch and gets about 3× slower under load: at 16 users first audio is about 2.4 s with 1–1.5 s of stutter. Check the server log for `Loaded flow-estimator TensorRT engine`. - **Recommended: up to 16 concurrent users per GPU.** More GPUs: one instance per GPU behind a load balancer; capacity scales roughly linearly. CPU is not a bottleneck (~1.5 cores per instance at 16 users). ## Sound tags `[laughter]`, `[breath]`, `[sigh]`, `[cough]`, `…` (laugh while speaking), `…` (stress a word). Tags are sent to the voice as whole chunks while text streams in, the same way the voice was trained. Event heard when the tag is written (96 test sentences × 2 runs through the full served pipeline, AST detector; 8–12 sentences per class, so ±1 sentence ≈ ±10 points): | | sigh | breath | cough | laugh | |---|---|---|---|---| | this release | 25% | 50% | 33% | 42% | | reference tag-tts renderer, same voice model | 42% | 50% | 33% | 50% | ## Live mode (OpenAI GPT-Live compatible) Run one more command next to the engine and GPT-Live clients can connect by changing only the URL and key. Sophon keeps the voice; when a request needs a lookup or an action it says "Let me check that", hands the task to your backend and speaks the result in its own words. ```bash cd sophon-realtime/live && BUILD=tag PORT=8000 LIVE_PORT=8780 bash start_live.sh # GPT-Live clients: ws://HOST:8780/v1/live/sessions ``` Details and measurements: [live/](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/live/README.md) in the GitHub repository. ## Fine-tuning Fine-tune the thinker's LLM backbone with LoRA in ms-swift to change persona, tone, domain knowledge and tool use. Hearing, the voice and turn-taking stay as released, and sound tags such as laughter and coughs are kept. One 80 GB GPU is enough; see [finetune/](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/finetune/README.md) in the GitHub repository. ## What's inside | folder | what | licence | |---|---|---| | `thinker/` | DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.5 with tag writing merged in, FP8 (with the vision tower) | Apache-2.0 | | `talker/` | tag-tts: language model + distilled flow (4 steps, no CFG) + HiFT; based on Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B | Apache-2.0 | | `voices/` | six reference voices (clip + precomputed prompt) | Apache-2.0 | ## Limitations - `[sigh]` and `…` are still weak; the thinker writes them more often than the voice delivers. - Mandarin is slightly less clear than English with the distilled flow; a laugh is sometimes transcribed as "哈哈" by ASR. - Very long replies (over about a minute of speech in one turn) are beyond what the voice was trained on.

Flash's voice stage is autoregressive with a single forward pass per step, so **first audio is faster and concurrency is higher**; the Tag build laughs more convincingly. Both have the same API. ## Sophon-Realtime v1 family Three builds share one brain (the same 32B model listens, decides turns and writes the reply). They differ only in how the reply becomes sound. Full comparison: [github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime). | | **Tag** (recommended) | **Flash** | **E2E** | |---|---|---|---| | How it speaks | an expressive speech model performs the sound tags | a lighter, faster speech model speaks the tagged reply | a compact talker (about 350M parameters) generates continuous voice vectors directly, no speech tokens | | NVV-SuperBench (en / zh) | **0.80 / 0.86** | 0.63 / 0.77 | 0.75 / 0.85 | | First audio, one user | ~0.6 s | 0.31 s | **~0.25 s** | | Users per 80 GB GPU (recommended) | 16 | **40** | 16 | | GPUs | 1 | 1 | 1 | | Weights | [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag) | [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash) | [Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E) | Pick **Tag** if you want the voice to act; pick **Flash** if users per GPU matter most; pick **E2E** for the fastest first audio with a voice that still laughs and sighs. Tag and Flash share the same APIs; E2E runs on its own engine or, since 1.1.4, on vLLM-Omni with the same APIs as Tag and Flash. ## Highlights - **VoiceBench 82.8 and Big Bench Audio 81.8%: the strongest brain among open full-duplex models.** #1 among open full-duplex models on both; level with GPT-4o-mini-Audio on VoiceBench. - **Paralinguistic understanding 48.6, #1 overall: it hears your tone.** Ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (46.9) and Qwen3-Omni (44.6) on LISTEN, StressTest and MSPB. It hears emotion, emphasis, sarcasm, laughter and sighs straight from your voice. - **Fast and the most scalable build: 0.31 s to first audio, up to 40 concurrent users per 80 GB GPU.** Made for customer service, in-car assistants and other many-user deployments. - **Still laughs and clears its throat: NVV-SuperBench 0.77 (Chinese) and 0.63 (English).** It speaks the same tagged replies as Tag with a lighter, faster voice. - **Full-Duplex-Bench v3 tool calling: Pass@1 48%, ahead of Grok (43%), with a 100% response rate.** Live mode is compatible with the OpenAI GPT-Live interface. - **Real full duplex.** It listens the whole time you talk and drafts its reply as you go; it picks up when you stop, stops when you cut in, and keeps going when you just say "mm-hm". - **Apache-2.0, free for commercial use.** Fine-tune persona, tone and domain knowledge with ms-swift. Benchmark methods and full comparison tables: [v1 family home page](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-v1). To just try it: [talk to it in the ModelScope Studio](https://www.modelscope.ai/studios/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime). ## Performance (one H100 80 GB, FP8 thinker, `/v1/chat/completions`, user speech → first audio chunk) | Load | First audio median / P90 | Stall (median) | |---|---|---| | 1 stream | **0.31 / 0.34 s** | 0 | | 20 streams (arriving over 10 s) | 0.45 / 0.52 s | 0.09 s | | 40 streams (over 10 s) | 0.58 / 0.67 s | 0.37 s | | 64 streams (over 8 s) | 0.84 / 1.03 s | 1.9 s (queueing) | - **Up to about 40 concurrent streams per 80 GB GPU is recommended.** For more, run one instance per GPU behind a load balancer. - Memory: about 55 GB per instance. The first start compiles kernels (about 10 min); later starts take 5–8 min. ### Sound tags (held-out set, Chelsie voice, judged by DuplexJev; not comparable with the AST hit rates on the Tag card — for a like-for-like comparison of the three builds, see NVV-SuperBench above) | Tag | zh | en | |---|---|---| | `[laughter]` | 83% | 77% | | `…` laughing while speaking | 78% | 71% | | `[cough]` | 90% | 50% (8 items) | | `[sigh]` (AST) | 90% | 100% | | Mean character / word error rate | 0.9% | 1.0% | - Tags are never read aloud; without a tag the model rarely laughs on its own. - `` emphasis is still weak in this build; the next build will improve it. ## Deployment code One-command scripts and the vLLM-Omni plugin: [github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/tree/main/flash](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/tree/main/flash). This repository holds the weights: `config.json`, `thinker/` (FP8), `talker/`, `voices/`. ## Quick start ```bash bash install.sh # once: Python 3.12 venv, vLLM 0.30, vLLM-Omni 0.30, plugin # put the weights in ./model (hf download adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash --local-dir ./model) GPU=0 PORT=8000 bash start.sh python client_example.py --wav my_question.wav --lang en --voice chelsie bash stop.sh ``` Voices: `chelsie` (default), `brand`; set `language` to `zh` or `en`. ## Zero-shot voice cloning Put a 3–10 s clip of one speaker at `model/voices/.wav` and use `"voice": ""` in `/v1/chat/completions` or `/v1/realtime`. No fine-tuning and no restart; first audio is as fast as with a built-in voice, and sound tags still work. Needs code version 1.1.0 or later; details in the [GitHub README](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/flash/README.md#zero-shot-voice-cloning). **Only clone your own voice or a voice you have permission to use. Do not use it to impersonate or deceive anyone.** ## API - `/v1/chat/completions`: use the system prompt in `config/system_prompt.json` (the model was tuned with it; without it fewer tags are written); put the user's speech in `input_audio`; `"modalities": ["text","audio"]`, optional `"voice"` and `"language"`. The text stream keeps the tags (strip them for display if you like); the audio stream is base64 WAV chunks (24 kHz). - `/v1/realtime`: OpenAI Realtime-style session; keep sending `input_audio_buffer.append`; the model decides when the user has finished. ## Live mode (OpenAI GPT-Live compatible) Run one more command next to the engine and GPT-Live clients can connect by changing only the URL and key. Sophon keeps the voice; when a request needs a lookup or an action it says "Let me check that", hands the task to your backend and speaks the result in its own words. ```bash cd sophon-realtime/live && BUILD=flash PORT=8000 LIVE_PORT=8780 bash start_live.sh # GPT-Live clients: ws://HOST:8780/v1/live/sessions ``` Details and measurements: [live/](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/live/README.md) in the GitHub repository. ## Fine-tuning Fine-tune the thinker's LLM backbone with LoRA in ms-swift to change persona, tone, domain knowledge and tool use. Hearing, the voice and turn-taking stay as released, and sound tags such as laughter and coughs are kept. One 80 GB GPU is enough; see [finetune/](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/finetune/README.md) in the GitHub repository. ## Layout `model/` (thinker, voice stage, voices) · `plugin/` (vLLM-Omni plugin `sophon_realtime`) · `config/` (deploy config, system prompt, VAD) · `examples/` License: code Apache-2.0; model weights Apache-2.0, see `NOTICE` for sources.

Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E

> 🎧 **Try it in your browser, no GPU and no sign-up:** [Sophon-Realtime on Hugging Face Spaces](https://huggingface.co/spaces/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime). Talk to it, interrupt it, turn on your camera.

Sophon-Realtime v1 系列的 E2E 版：单卡、首包约 0.25 秒，声音直接从连续向量里生成
AI降临派（Adventists AI）· Apache-2.0 · v1.3.0

GitHub · Hugging Face · 魔搭 · English

## 这是什么 Sophon-Realtime 是全双工语音对话模型：一个 32B 的大脑负责听你说话、判断你说完没有、写出带声音标签的回复。E2E 版负责把回复变成声音的部分不经过语音 token：一个小巧的说话头（约 3.5 亿参数）在大脑还在写回复时就开始读，边读边生成连续的声音向量（每秒约 6.5 帧），再由 2 步解码器和声码器还原成 24 kHz 音频。笑、咳嗽、叹气、呼吸和重读都由说话头自己在同一条流里发出来。 整套系统（大脑 + 说话头 + 解码器）跑在**一张 80 GB 显卡**上。 ## 1.3.0 更新（2026-11-14） - E2E 版支持零样本音色克隆：给一段 5–12 秒的录音，按名字使用即可，无需微调、无需重启（vLLM-Omni 部署方式，需要代码 1.3.0 及以上）。用法见下面的[音色克隆](#音色克隆)。权重没有变化。 ## 1.2.0 更新（2026-11-13） - 长回复会完整说完，不再限制语音时长（之前约 2 到 2.5 分钟就在句末收住）：说话头把长回复分成约 25–40 秒一段来说，每段都从剩下的文字重新开始。实测在 vLLM-Omni 部署方式下最长说到约 14 分钟。权重没有变化。详见[更新记录](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)。 ## 1.1.4 更新（2026-11-12） - E2E 版现在也可以像 Tag、Flash 一样作为一个 vLLM-Omni 模型来部署（代码在 [`e2e/`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/e2e/README_CN.md)），命令、接口（`/v1/realtime`、`/v1/chat/completions`）和客户端都相同。自研引擎的部署方式不变，速度略快。 - 本仓库新增 `thinker/`（已合并回复 LoRA 的大脑，FP8，约 36 GB，与 Tag 仓库里的是同一份文件）、`config.json` 和 `talker220/config.json`，只有 vLLM-Omni 部署方式用到。其他文件没有变化。 - 两种部署方式各自只下载自己需要的部分：自研引擎约 67 GB（不含 `thinker/`），vLLM-Omni 约 41 GB（不含 `base/`、`adapters/`）；安装脚本会自动处理。 ## 1.1.3 更新（2026-11-11） - 与 Tag、Flash 并列为正式版本，从两张卡变成一张卡。 - 新的说话头（`talker220/`），原来的 `talker/` 已移除，下载量少约 8 GB；`base/`、`adapters/`、`e2/`、`voices/` 没有变化。 - 之前的双卡权重保留在本仓库的 `v1.1.0` 标签下（配合代码标签 `v1.1.2` 使用）。 ## 在 v1 系列里的位置 三个版本是同一个大脑（VoiceBench 82.8、Big Bench Audio 81.8%，两项开源全双工第一；副语言理解综合第一），区别只在回复怎么变成声音： | | [Tag](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag)（推荐） | [Flash](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash) | **E2E（本仓库）** | |---|---|---|---| | NVV-SuperBench（英 / 中） | **0.80 / 0.86** | 0.63 / 0.77 | 0.75 / 0.85 | | 单路首包 | 约 0.6 秒 | 0.31 秒 | **约 0.25 秒** | | 每张 80 GB 卡建议并发 | 16 路 | **40 路** | 16 路 | | 零样本音色克隆 | 支持 | 支持 | 支持（vLLM-Omni 部署方式） | | 语言 | 中、英和多种欧洲语言 | 同左，另有日、俄 | 中、英 | | 部署 | vLLM-Omni | vLLM-Omni | 自研引擎或 vLLM-Omni | 想要更多语言，用 Tag 或 Flash；想要最快的首包、同时保留会笑会叹气的表现力，用 E2E。 ## 实测（单张 H100 80 GB，全新安装） 语音提问进、语音回答出，全链路都在同一张卡上。首包指从发出请求到收到第一块音频。 | 10 秒内到达的用户数 | 首包 中位数 / P90 | 播放落后超过 0.3 秒的回复数 | |---|---|---| | 1 | 0.25 秒 | 0 | | 8 | 0.44 / 0.77 秒 | 0 / 8 | | **16** | **0.44 / 0.56 秒** | **0 / 16** | | 24 | 0.58 / 0.94 秒 | 7 / 24 | | 32 | 0.67 / 0.80 秒 | 23 / 32 | NVV-SuperBench（官方题目与指标，每类每种语言 50 条，Gemini 3 Flash 裁判，F1）： | | 四类合计 | 笑 | 咳嗽 | 叹气 | 呼吸 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 英文 | 0.75 | 0.70 | 0.76 | 0.92 | 0.64 | | 中文 | 0.85 | 0.86 | 0.95 | 0.87 | 0.74 | 同一批句子的转写错字率：中文 3.1%，英文 1.9%。 ## 部署 需要 Linux、NVIDIA 驱动 580 及以上、一张 H100 级的 80 GB 显卡（实际占用约 70 GB）。有两种方式，权重相同、声音相同。 **方式一：自研引擎**（上面表格里的数字） ```bash git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime cd sophon-realtime bash scripts/install.sh # 建两个虚拟环境，并从魔搭下载本模型 SOPHON_MODEL_DIR=$PWD/Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E GPU=0 bash scripts/start.sh ``` 启动后打开 `http://<服务器>:8000/` 即可在网页里直接对话，也可以通过 WebSocket 接口（`/ws`）接入自己的客户端。详见 [docs/deploy_CN.md](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/docs/deploy_CN.md)。 **方式二：vLLM-Omni**（与 Tag、Flash 相同的命令和接口） ```bash git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime && cd sophon-realtime/e2e bash install.sh # 建虚拟环境，并从魔搭下载本模型中需要的部分（约 41 GB） GPU=0 PORT=8000 bash start.sh python client_example.py --wav my_question.wav --lang zh ``` 提供 `ws://<服务器>:8000/v1/realtime`（全双工）和 `/v1/chat/completions`。单张 H100 实测：单路首包约 0.35 秒；16 路首包中位数 0.58–0.65 秒、P90 0.71–0.87 秒，0–2 路回复播放落后超过 0.3 秒；全双工下从说完到出声中位数约 0.45 秒。详见 [e2e/README_CN.md](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/e2e/README_CN.md)。 **其他显卡**：以上数字都是在 H100 上测的。在一张 RTX PRO 6000（Blackwell，96 GB）上实测 vLLM-Omni 方式：能安装、能运行，但一张卡只能跟上约 4–8 路并发（E2E 发声部分在这张卡上慢约一倍）。在这类显卡上需要更高并发时，请用 Tag 或 Flash。 ## 音色克隆 需要代码 1.3.0 及以上，vLLM-Omni 部署方式（GitHub 仓库的 `e2e/`）。把录音放进 `model/voices/`，按名字使用： ```bash cp alice.wav model/voices/alice.wav # 5–12 秒、只有一个人说话的清晰录音（wav 或 flac，16 kHz 及以上） python client_example.py --wav my_question.wav --lang zh --voice alice ``` - 需要 Tag 发布包里的两个小模型 `speech_tokenizer_v3.onnx` 和 `campplus.onnx`（约 1 GB），`install.sh` 会自动下载到 `model/clone_frontend/talker/`；本仓库的权重不需要改动。 - 第一次用到时准备并缓存，首包和内置音色一样快；录音太短或读不了时回落内置音色。 - 详细说明见 [e2e/README_CN.md](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/e2e/README_CN.md)。 - **请只克隆自己的声音，或已获得声音主人许可的声音；不得用于冒充他人或欺诈。** ## 声音标签 `[laughter]` `[cough]` `[sigh]` `[breath]`（在该位置发出声音）、`词`（重读）、`几个词`（边笑边说）。大脑会自己把它们写进回复；说话头把它们演出来，不会念出来。 ## 这一版的限制 - 一个内置音色；音色克隆只在 vLLM-Omni 部署方式下可用（自研引擎方式暂不支持）。 - 回复用中文或英文。 - 单条回复最长约 4.6 分钟语音（vLLM-Omni 方式约 2.5 分钟）；超出时这条回复在该处正常结束，不影响其他对话。连续说到约 2.5 分钟以内内容是准确的，更长的回复后段会出现念错，建议把单条回复控制在 2.5 分钟以内。 ## 文件 | 目录 | 内容 | |---|---| | `base/` | 大脑的 32B 权重 | | `adapters/tag/` | 写带标签回复的 LoRA | | `talker220/` | 说话头：权重、文字嵌入表、分词器 | | `e2/` | 解码器与声码器 | | `voices/` | 默认音色 | | `thinker/`、`config.json`、`talker220/config.json` | 只有 vLLM-Omni 部署方式用到：已合并回复 LoRA 的大脑（FP8，约 36 GB） | ## 许可证 代码和权重都是 Apache-2.0。第三方组件保留各自的许可证，见 GitHub 仓库的 [NOTICE](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/NOTICE)。 ## 联系 商务合作：jiejin@adventists.ai --- # Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E > **No GPU?** Try it through the hosted API: [sign up](https://api.adventists.ai/console/) and get 3 hours of free voice chat (OpenAI Realtime-compatible, [docs](https://api.adventists.ai/console/docs)). > 🆕 **Smaller GPU?** [Sophon-Realtime-4B-E2E](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-4B-E2E) (v1.4.0) runs this build with a 4B brain on one 32 GB GPU: keeps the turn-taking and sound tags, knows much less. [All builds](https://huggingface.co/collections/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime-6afb357253a3a8905ad758b0) **The E2E build of the Sophon-Realtime v1 family: one GPU, first audio in about 0.25 s, speech generated directly as continuous vectors.** Adventists AI · Apache-2.0 · v1.3.0 ## What it is Sophon-Realtime is a full-duplex voice model: a 32B brain listens to you, decides when you have finished, and writes a reply with sound tags. In the E2E build, the part that turns the reply into sound has no speech-token model in the middle. A compact talker (about 350M parameters) reads the reply while it is still being written and generates a stream of continuous voice vectors, about 6.5 frames per second; a 2-step decoder and a vocoder turn them into 24 kHz audio. Laughs, coughs, sighs, breaths and stressed words are produced by the talker itself, as part of the same stream. The whole system (brain, talker, decoder) runs on **one 80 GB GPU**. ## What's new in 1.3.0 (2026-11-14) - E2E now does zero-shot voice cloning: give it a 5–12 s clip and use the voice by name, with no fine-tuning and no restart (vLLM-Omni deployment, requires code 1.3.0 or later). See [Voice cloning](#voice-cloning) below. The weights are unchanged. ## What's new in 1.2.0 (2026-11-13) - Long replies are spoken to their end, with no limit on speech length (before, speech ended at a sentence end after about 2 to 2.5 minutes): the talker speaks them in segments of about 25–40 s, each a fresh start on the rest of the text. Tested up to about 14 minutes with the vLLM-Omni deployment. The weights are unchanged. See the [changelog](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). ## What's new in 1.1.4 (2026-11-12) - E2E can now also be served as one vLLM-Omni model, like Tag and Flash (code in [`e2e/`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/e2e/README.md)), with the same commands, APIs (`/v1/realtime`, `/v1/chat/completions`) and client. The own-engine deployment is unchanged and a little faster. - New in this repository: `thinker/` (the brain with the reply LoRA merged in, FP8, about 36 GB; the same files as in the Tag repository), `config.json` and `talker220/config.json`. Only the vLLM-Omni deployment uses them. Nothing else changed. - Each way of deploying downloads only what it needs: about 67 GB for the own engine (without `thinker/`), about 41 GB for vLLM-Omni (without `base/` and `adapters/`). The install scripts take care of it. ## What's new in 1.1.3 (2026-11-11) - A full build next to Tag and Flash, on one GPU instead of two. - New talker (`talker220/`); the old `talker/` is removed, so the download is about 8 GB smaller. `base/`, `adapters/`, `e2/` and `voices/` are unchanged. - The earlier two-GPU weights stay in this repository at tag `v1.1.0` (use them with code tag `v1.1.2`). ## Where it fits in the v1 family All three builds share one brain (VoiceBench 82.8 and Big Bench Audio 81.8%, #1 among open full-duplex models on both; #1 in paralinguistic understanding). They differ only in how the reply becomes sound: | | [Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag) (recommended) | [Flash](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash) | **E2E (this repository)** | |---|---|---|---| | NVV-SuperBench (en / zh) | **0.80 / 0.86** | 0.63 / 0.77 | 0.75 / 0.85 | | First audio, one user | ~0.6 s | 0.31 s | **~0.25 s** | | Recommended users per 80 GB GPU | 16 | **40** | 16 | | Zero-shot voice cloning | yes | yes | yes (vLLM-Omni deployment) | | Languages | Chinese, English and several European languages | the same, plus Japanese and Russian | Chinese, English | | Serving | vLLM-Omni | vLLM-Omni | own engine or vLLM-Omni | Use Tag or Flash for more languages; use E2E for the fastest first audio with a voice that still laughs and sighs. ## Measured (one H100 80 GB, fresh install) Spoken question in, spoken answer out, everything on the same GPU. First audio is the time from sending the request to receiving the first audio chunk. | Users arriving within 10 s | First audio, median / P90 | Replies whose playback fell more than 0.3 s behind | |---|---|---| | 1 | 0.25 s | 0 | | 8 | 0.44 / 0.77 s | 0 of 8 | | **16** | **0.44 / 0.56 s** | **0 of 16** | | 24 | 0.58 / 0.94 s | 7 of 24 | | 32 | 0.67 / 0.80 s | 23 of 32 | NVV-SuperBench (official prompts and metric, 50 items per class per language, Gemini 3 Flash judge, F1): | | All 4 | Laugh | Cough | Sigh | Breath | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | English | 0.75 | 0.70 | 0.76 | 0.92 | 0.64 | | Chinese | 0.85 | 0.86 | 0.95 | 0.87 | 0.74 | Transcription error rate on the same sentences: Chinese 3.1%, English 1.9%. ## Deployment Linux, NVIDIA driver 580 or newer, one 80 GB GPU of the H100 class (about 70 GB is used). There are two ways, with the same weights and the same voice. **1. Own engine** (the numbers in the tables above) ```bash git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime cd sophon-realtime bash scripts/install.sh # two virtual environments + this model from ModelScope SOPHON_MODEL_DIR=$PWD/Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E GPU=0 bash scripts/start.sh ``` Then open `http://:8000/` to talk in the browser, or connect your own client to the WebSocket API (`/ws`). See [docs/deploy.md](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/docs/deploy.md). **2. vLLM-Omni** (the same commands and APIs as Tag and Flash) ```bash git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime && cd sophon-realtime/e2e bash install.sh # virtual environment + the parts of this model it needs, from ModelScope (about 41 GB) GPU=0 PORT=8000 bash start.sh python client_example.py --wav my_question.wav --lang en ``` It serves `ws://:8000/v1/realtime` (full duplex) and `/v1/chat/completions`. Measured on one H100: first audio about 0.35 s for one user; 16 users 0.58–0.65 s median / 0.71–0.87 s P90, with 0–2 replies falling more than 0.3 s behind playback; in full duplex about 0.45 s (median) from the end of your speech to the first voice. See [e2e/README.md](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/e2e/README.md). **Other GPUs:** all numbers above are measured on an H100. On one RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell, 96 GB) the vLLM-Omni deployment installs and runs, but one GPU keeps up with only about 4–8 concurrent users (the E2E voice stages run about 2× slower on that card). If you need more users per GPU on such cards, use Tag or Flash. ## Voice cloning Requires code 1.3.0 or later and the vLLM-Omni deployment (`e2e/` in the GitHub repository). Put a clip in `model/voices/` and use it by name: ```bash cp alice.wav model/voices/alice.wav # 5-12 s of clean speech from one speaker (wav or flac, 16 kHz or more) python client_example.py --wav my_question.wav --lang en --voice alice ``` - It needs two small models from the Tag release, `speech_tokenizer_v3.onnx` and `campplus.onnx` (about 1 GB); `install.sh` downloads them to `model/clone_frontend/talker/`. The brain writes them into the reply on its own; the talker performs them instead of reading them aloud. ## Limits of this release - One built-in voice; voice cloning works only with the vLLM-Omni deployment (not yet with the own engine). - Replies are spoken in Chinese or English. - One reply can be at most about 4.6 minutes of speech (about 2.5 minutes with vLLM-Omni); a longer reply ends cleanly at that point and other conversations are not affected. # Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash-4bit-MLX

> 🎧 **Try it in your browser, no GPU and no sign-up:** [Sophon-Realtime on Hugging Face Spaces](https://huggingface.co/spaces/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime). Talk to it, interrupt it, turn on your camera.


> **No GPU?** Try it through the hosted API: [sign up](https://api.adventists.ai/console/) and get 3 hours of free voice chat (OpenAI Realtime-compatible, [docs](https://api.adventists.ai/console/docs)).


**Version 1.2.0** · [changelog](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) · code: [`mac/`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/tree/main/mac) · CUDA build: [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash-4bit](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash-4bit) · 中文：`README_CN.md`

The full-duplex speech model [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash-4bit](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash-4bit), **running locally on an Apple silicon Mac** with MLX.
You talk, it decides by itself when you have finished, answers with its own voice and sound tags, stops when you interrupt, and carries on when you
just say "mm-hmm". Hearing, turn-taking and speaking are all done by the model on the Mac's GPU: no cloud, and no speech-to-text step in between.

The weights are the Flash-4bit weights **repacked losslessly** for MLX: the 4-bit values, scales, audio tower and voice stage are bit-identical to the CUDA build.

## Requirements
- Apple silicon (M1 or later), macOS 14 or later
- **36 GB or more unified memory recommended**; 32 GB works with other apps closed (about 26 GB in use while talking)
- About 24 GB download
- A microphone. Mac Studio and Mac mini have none built in: plug in a USB microphone or a headset. Speakers are fine, echo cancellation is built in

## Quick start
```bash
git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime && cd sophon-realtime
bash mac/install.sh            # Python environment + this repo's weights, into ~/sophon-mac
~/sophon-mac/sophon            # talk in Chinese
~/sophon-mac/sophon --lang en  # talk in English
```
Options: `--no-aec` (headset, no echo cancellation), `--in` / `--out` (audio devices, `--list` shows them), `--voice`.

## Speed (M4 Max, 36 GB)
| | |
|---|---|
| You stop talking → it starts speaking | **0.9–1.1 s** when the model is sure you have finished; up to about 2.5 s when it waits to see whether you go on |
| Long replies | real time, no stalls |
| You interrupt | it stops within about 0.15 s |
| Model load | about 10 s |

The CUDA server answers in about 0.5 s. On a Mac most of the time goes into the turn decision: when you pause, the model listens to your whole
utterance once on the Mac's GPU. Chips with more GPU cores are faster.

## How turn-taking works on a Mac
To process your audio only once, the turn question is asked inside the reply's own context (system prompt, conversation, your audio, then a short
"has the user finished? A / B" question); if the answer is yes, the reply continues from the same computation. The check schedule and thresholds are
those of the server (0.2 s to 2 s of silence, then a fallback reply). Accuracy on the Smart Turn test set (400 clips per language):

| | English acc. / AUC | Chinese acc. / AUC |
|---|---|---|
| Server turn question | 92.5 / 0.975 | 94.0 / 0.983 |
| **Mac turn question** | **90.5 / 0.960** | **94.3 / 0.977** |

Right after you interrupt, the full four-option question is used instead, so that a short back-channel ("mm-hmm", "yeah") makes it resume the cut reply.

## Echo cancellation
WebRTC AEC3 removes the reply's own sound from the microphone. In a simulated room (speaker sound back at the microphone at −6 dB and 0 dB, 6 s of
reply), the reply never interrupted itself with echo cancellation on (3 / 3 runs) and did every time with it off; a real interruption was still
detected within about 0.12 s.

## Status and limits
- Tested on an M4 Max (36 GB) with real-time simulated audio input (speech played into the engine at real-time pace, simulated room echo).
  Live microphone runs and numbers from other Macs are very welcome in [issue #1](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/issues/1).
- One conversation at a time. Camera input, tool calls and zero-shot voice cloning are not in the Mac version yet (built-in voices only).

## Files
| Folder | What |
|---|---|
| `thinker_mlx/` | the 4-bit thinker for `mlx_lm` (same weights as Flash-4bit) |
| `ear/` | the thinker's audio tower and projector |
| `talker/` | the voice stage (same as Flash) |
| `voices/` | built-in voices |
